newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire capital agog at opposition leader's remarks.
newsitem.headline: Zaire capital agog at opposition leader's remarks.

text.p: Radical opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi's "reconciliation" in France with Zaire's veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, his one-time friend and long-time foe, raised eyebrows and blood pressure on Friday in the capital Kinshasa.
Tshisekedi told Radio France International on Friday that Mobutu, who is in southern France recuperating from cancer surgery, had given him a mandate to form a national unity government.
Mobutu's spokesman in Kinshasa, Professor Kabuya Lumuna, expressed astonishment.

"Mr Tshisekedi's obsession is to be prime minister. The obsession of every other Zairean at the moment is to win the war in the east," he told Reuters. "Clearly he has taken his own thoughts for the thoughts of the president."
Tshisekedi, speaking after talks with Mobutu late on Thursday, said dialogue was the only way to end a revolt by Tutsi and other Mobutu opponents who hold towns in the east.

"It must be resolved through negotiation because we have already shed too much blood of our people," he said, playing down the role of neighbouring Rwanda and adding that the month-old revolt was essentially an internal problem.

Tshisekedi's supporters among students in Kinshasa have been at the forefront of a campaign against part-Tutsi Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo and spearheading demands that the army be given the means to impose a military solution.

Tshisekedi said rebel leader Laurent Kabila, another veteran Mobutu foe, should have a role in Zaire as he too was party to the decisions of a 1992 sovereign national conference which Mobutu had re-endorsed.

The conference, which effectively launched Zaire's much-delayed democratic transition, elected Tshisekedi prime minister in 1992 but Mobutu shunted him aside in 1993, a decision Tshisekedi has always refused to accept.
"With this reconciliation that we have just had, President Mobutu... will respect the constitutional act so that I lead what we call a government of national unity," Tshisekedi said.
His comments made waves at home, not least in Kengo's camp.

"You cannot go to Cap-Martin to be appointed prime minister. You must be elected by parliament in Zaire and only after Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo has been voted out," Tharcisse Loseke Nembalemba, leader of Kengo's Union of Independent Democrats in the transitional parliament, commented.
Political opponents say Tshisekedi's "national reconciliation" has not been endorsed by any member of Mobutu's political family.
Other commentators suspect Mobutu may have made promises to his rival in order to embarrass him politically ahead of presidential and other elections to be held by July 1997.

"In politics everything is possible. Mobutu can tell Tshisekedi he is prime minister and then straight away ask his advisor to deny it so as to make Tshisekedi look foolish," Honore Kilak, a leading youth activist, said.
Tshisekedi's call for dialogue in the east found little echo in Kinshasa where the government and students in the streets have been calling for a military solution.

But some Western diplomats in Kinshasa favour a negotiated solution. "There are supposed to be elections in Zaire next year. If Kabila really is popular in the east then he should be encouraged to stand in them," one said.
